section.title: The Line of Ishmael
section.sectionRationale: Before the story narrows to Isaac and his sons, Scripture pauses to honour God's promise to Ishmael. Twelve princes are born to him, just as God had said, a reminder that God keeps even His secondary promises, and that His care reaches beyond the chosen line.
section.thesis: God faithfully keeps His word to Ishmael, making him fruitful with twelve princes, even as the covenant line runs on through Isaac; God's promises never fall to the ground, and His mercy extends beyond the chosen line.
section.frameNote: Two scenes: the twelve sons of Ishmael listed; Ishmael's death and the territory of his descendants.

units.label: The twelve sons of Ishmael
units.note: twelve princes, as God had promised

verses.text: This is the {{toledot|account}} of Abraham’s son Ishmael, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s maidservant, bore to Abraham.
These are the names of the sons of Ishmael in the order of their birth: Nebaioth the firstborn of Ishmael, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam,
Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.
These were the sons of Ishmael, and these were their names by their villages and encampments, twelve {{nasi|princes}} of their tribes.

units.label: Ishmael's death and territory
units.note: settled near the border of Egypt

verses.text: Ishmael lived a total of 137 years. Then he breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people.
Ishmael’s descendants settled from Havilah to Shur, which is near the border of Egypt as you go toward Asshur. And they lived in {{hostility|hostility}} toward all their brothers.

toledot.gloss: Generations, account, or family record, from a root meaning to bear or bring forth. It is the structural key of Genesis, marking off its major sections with the phrase this is the account of. Here a brief toledot of Ishmael honours him before the narrative turns fully to the line of Isaac.

nasi.gloss: A chief, leader, or prince, one lifted up to rule a tribe or people. Ishmael's twelve sons become twelve princes, echoing the promise God made to Hagar and to Abraham. The number twelve deliberately mirrors the twelve tribes of Israel, marking Ishmael as a great people in his own right.

hostility.gloss: To fall, settle, or dwell, here in an idiom for living over against or in defiance of others. The phrase describes Ishmael's descendants settling apart from, and in tension with, their kin, fulfilling the earlier word that he would live at odds with his brothers, yet still within reach of God's care.

basic.context: Just after Abraham's death, before the story focuses on Isaac's sons, Scripture records Ishmael's line. He fathers twelve sons who become twelve tribal princes, exactly as God had promised Hagar and Abraham. Then his death and the region his descendants settled are noted. The key question is why the chosen line pauses to honour Ishmael.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a genealogical record with a theological point: God keeps His promises, including the ones made to those outside the main covenant line. The interpreter should read the twelve princes as a deliberate fulfilment, not a random list, and notice God's faithfulness and mercy reaching beyond Isaac.
basic.originalLanguages: The section opens with toledot, the account or generations, the structural marker of Genesis. Ishmael's sons become twelve nasi, princes, mirroring Israel's twelve tribes. The closing note uses an idiom, naphal, of settling over against one's brothers, describing a people apart yet still remembered by God.
basic.typology: Ishmael blessed yet not the covenant heir illustrates the pattern Paul draws out: the child of the flesh and the child of promise. His genuine blessing shows God's kindness, while the promise runs on through Isaac, pointing to the line that leads to Christ.
basic.christ: The narrowing from Abraham's many descendants to Isaac, and later to one line, moves toward Christ, the true seed. Yet the honouring of Ishmael foreshadows the wideness of God's mercy, which in Christ reaches even the outsider and the far off.
basic.god: God is faithful to every word He speaks. He had promised to make Ishmael fruitful and to bring twelve princes from him, and He does. He cares for those outside the chosen line, hearing Hagar and blessing her son, showing a mercy broader than one family.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 17 and 21 record God's promise to make Ishmael a great nation with twelve princes. Galatians 4 contrasts the son of the slave and the son of promise. Romans 9 speaks of God's sovereign choice within Abraham's line.
basic.oneStory: God keeps His promise to Ishmael even as He carries the covenant through Isaac. It is a small witness that God's word never fails and His mercy is wide, while the main story moves on toward the promised seed, Christ.

context.literary:
This short passage is one of the toledot sections that give Genesis its shape. The formula 'This is the account of' opens it, verse 12, as it opened the accounts of the heavens and the earth, Genesis 2:4, Noah, Genesis 6:9, and Terah, Genesis 11:27. It is followed at once by 'This is the account of Abraham's son Isaac,' verse 19. The two headings stand side by side, and both sons are called 'Abraham's son.' The narrator gives Ishmael his own heading, his own genealogy and his own death notice before the story moves on.

The passage has a simple frame. It opens with Ishmael's origin, 'whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's maidservant, bore to Abraham,' verse 12, a line that recalls Genesis 16:1 and 16:15. It lists twelve names in birth order, verses 13 to 15, and summarises them as 'twelve princes of their tribes,' verse 16. It records Ishmael's lifespan and death in exactly the formula just used for Abraham, verse 17 and verse 8. And it closes with the territory and character of his descendants, verse 18.

This is a pattern Genesis uses throughout. The line that does not carry the covenant is dealt with first, briefly and respectfully, and then the narrative returns to the chosen line at length. Cain's descendants are listed, Genesis 4:17-24, before Seth's line, Genesis 5. Japheth and Ham come before Shem in the Table of Nations, Genesis 10. Ishmael comes before Isaac here, and Esau's long genealogy in Genesis 36 comes before 'the account of Jacob,' Genesis 37:2. The effect is not to dismiss the other lines but to show that God's promises to them are kept, and then to narrow the reader's attention to the line of promise.

The closing words of verse 18 tie the passage back to the angel's word to Hagar, 'he will live in hostility toward all his brothers,' Genesis 16:12. Ishmael's story in Genesis began with a prophecy before his birth, and it ends with the narrator noting its fulfilment.
context.historical:
The names in verses 13 to 15 point to peoples and places of northern Arabia and the Syrian desert. Several appear in later Scripture and in ancient records. Kedar became the most prominent. Isaiah speaks of 'the glory of Kedar' and its archers, Isaiah 21:16-17, Ezekiel of 'the princes of Kedar' trading in lambs and goats, Ezekiel 27:21, and Jeremiah of Kedar's tents, flocks and camels, Jeremiah 49:28-29. Assyrian and Babylonian records also mention the Qedarites as a powerful Arabian people. Tema is the oasis of northwestern Arabia later known as Tayma, famous as a caravan stop, Job 6:19 and Isaiah 21:14, and the place where the Babylonian king Nabonidus spent several years. Dumah is often identified with the oasis of Dumat al Jandal, and Isaiah has an oracle concerning it, Isaiah 21:11. Jetur is often connected with the Ituraeans of Luke 3:1, and Jetur and Naphish appear as enemies of the Transjordan tribes, 1 Chronicles 5:19.

The summary 'by their villages and encampments,' verse 16, describes a people partly settled and partly mobile. Villages were unwalled settlements; encampments were the camps of herders who moved with their flocks. The Ishmaelites were caravan traders, as the scene of Joseph's sale shows: 'a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead' with camels carrying spices, balm and myrrh to Egypt, Genesis 37:25.

The territory 'from Havilah to Shur, which is near the border of Egypt as you go toward Asshur,' verse 18, marks out the desert between Egypt and Mesopotamia. The same phrase 'from Havilah to Shur' describes the range of the Amalekites in 1 Samuel 15:7. Shur is the region where the angel first found Hagar, 'the spring along the road to Shur,' Genesis 16:7. The BSB footnote notes that Asshur may mean Assyria.

Ishmael lived to 137, verse 17. He was fourteen years older than Isaac, Genesis 16:16 and 21:5, and later Jewish and Islamic tradition came to regard him as the ancestor of many Arab peoples.
context.canonical:
The passage is the fulfilment of promises made in three earlier chapters. The angel told Hagar, 'I will greatly multiply your offspring so that they will be too numerous to count,' Genesis 16:10. God told Abraham, 'As for Ishmael, I have heard you, and I will surely bless him... He will become the father of twelve rulers, and I will make him into a great nation,' Genesis 17:20. And when Hagar and the boy were sent away, God said, 'I will also make a nation of the slave woman's son, because he is your offspring,' Genesis 21:13, and 'I will make him into a great nation,' Genesis 21:18. Genesis 25:12-18 shows all of it done.

Ishmael's line reappears in Israel's story. Esau marries 'Mahalath, the sister of Nebaioth and daughter of Abraham's son Ishmael,' Genesis 28:9, also called Basemath, Genesis 36:3. The Ishmaelites carry Joseph into Egypt, Genesis 37:25-28 and 39:1. In Gideon's time the Midianite raiders are described as 'Ishmaelites' because of their gold earrings, Judges 8:24. Psalm 83:6 lists 'the Ishmaelites' among the nations allied against God's people. The record of the chronicler repeats the list of Ishmael's sons, 1 Chronicles 1:29-31.

The prophets look to Ishmael's descendants with judgment and with hope. Isaiah announces the end of 'the glory of Kedar,' Isaiah 21:16. Yet Isaiah also calls on 'the villages of Kedar' to sing a new song to the LORD, Isaiah 42:11, and sees 'the flocks of Kedar' and 'the rams of Nebaioth' going up on God's altar 'with acceptance,' Isaiah 60:7.

In the New Testament, Paul uses Ishmael and Isaac to illustrate two covenants, the son 'born according to the flesh' and the son 'born through the promise,' Galatians 4:22-31, and he insists that 'Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned,' Romans 9:7. Yet at Pentecost 'Arabs' are among those who hear the wonders of God in their own tongues, Acts 2:11.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to know that God keeps every word He speaks, including words spoken to people outside the covenant line. God had promised Hagar numberless offspring, Genesis 16:10, and Abraham twelve princes from Ishmael, Genesis 17:20. Israel, living alongside the Ishmaelite peoples of the desert, could see the proof of God's faithfulness in their very neighbours. If God kept His lesser promises to Ishmael, how much more would He keep His covenant promises to Isaac.

He also wanted Israel to understand its neighbours. The peoples of the desert fringe, Kedar, Tema, Dumah and the rest, were Israel's relatives. They were not strangers but descendants of Abraham, and their hostility, verse 18, had been foretold before Ishmael was born. Israel was to see that its relationship with those peoples was part of a story God had been directing all along.

Finally, the author wanted Israel to see that divine election is not divine neglect. Ishmael is not the child of the covenant, Genesis 17:21, yet he is blessed, fruitful, honoured with his own toledot, and given the same dignified death notice as Abraham. God's choice of Isaac does not mean contempt for Ishmael. The passage teaches Israel to hold together its own chosenness and God's genuine care for the nations.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes the descendants of Ishmael, their settlements and their territory. It commands nothing, and its list of tribes and places is historical record rather than instruction.

What it teaches by example concerns God's character and His people's attitude. God keeps His word to those outside the covenant, so His people should never assume that God is indifferent to other nations. Believers are called to a similar breadth, to pray 'for everyone,' because God 'wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth,' 1 Timothy 2:1-4.

The passage also warns against using it to fuel national or ethnic hostility. The note that Ishmael's descendants 'lived in hostility toward all their brothers,' verse 18, describes what happened; it does not sanction it, and it does not define any modern people. Paul's use of Ishmael in Galatians 4 is about two ways of relating to God, by the flesh or by promise, not about ethnicity. The gospel invites the sons of Kedar and Nebaioth, as it invites everyone, into the one family of Abraham by faith, Galatians 3:7.

debates.question: Why does Genesis give space to Ishmael's line at all, since the covenant runs through Isaac?

views.label: To show God keeps His promises to Ishmael
views.case: God had explicitly pledged twelve princes and a great nation, Genesis 17:20 and 21:18. Recording them proves His word reliable even outside the chosen line, and honours Abraham's son with his own toledot heading.

views.label: To set the covenant line in relief
views.case: Genesis regularly closes off the non chosen branch before returning to the chosen one, as with Cain, Japheth and Ham, and Esau. The brief notice clears the stage so that the narrative can concentrate on Isaac and his sons.

views.label: To explain Israel's neighbours
views.case: Israel lived beside the Arabian peoples named here. The genealogy tells Israel who they are and why they live as they do, and it traces their hostility to a word spoken before Ishmael's birth.

debates.bearing: All three are true. The passage magnifies God's faithfulness to Ishmael, clears the way for the covenant story, and helps Israel understand its world, all in seven verses.

debates.question: What does the closing clause of verse 18 mean?

views.label: They lived in hostility toward their brothers
views.case: The BSB and many modern translations take the phrase as the fulfilment of Genesis 16:12, 'he will live in hostility toward all his brothers.' The same expression 'over against all his brothers' appears in both verses, and the narrator closes Ishmael's story by showing the prophecy come true.

views.label: They settled alongside or east of their brothers
views.case: The Hebrew phrase can also describe position, 'in front of' or 'east of.' On this reading the verse is geographical: Ishmael's descendants settled on the desert border, facing the lands of their relatives. The previous clause, which gives the boundaries of their territory, supports a geographical sense.

views.label: He died in the presence of his brothers
views.case: The verb in the clause is naphal, literally 'to fall.' Older translations, including the King James Version, took it as 'he died in the presence of all his brethren,' continuing the death notice of verse 17.

debates.bearing: The echo of Genesis 16:12 is strong, and the closing of a story with the fulfilment of its opening prophecy is typical of Genesis. Whether hostility or location is stressed, the narrator is showing that God's word about Ishmael came true in every part, both the blessing and the hard edge.

debates.question: Does Ishmael's line stand outside God's saving purposes?

views.label: Blessed, but outside the covenant
views.case: God said clearly, 'I will establish My covenant with Isaac,' Genesis 17:21, and Paul writes that 'the slave woman's son will never share in the inheritance,' Galatians 4:30. Ishmael receives temporal blessing, but the saving promise runs through Isaac.

views.label: Outside for now, invited later
views.case: The prophets see Ishmael's descendants coming to worship: Kedar sings a new song, Isaiah 42:11, and the rams of Nebaioth go up on God's altar with acceptance, Isaiah 60:7. At Pentecost Arabs hear the gospel, Acts 2:11. The covenant runs through Isaac, but its blessing is for all families of the earth, Genesis 12:3.

debates.bearing: Both are true at different points of the story. The covenant is carried by Isaac's line and comes to its fulfilment in Christ, and through Christ the descendants of Ishmael, like all nations, are invited in by faith. Paul's contrast in Galatians 4 concerns the way of the flesh and the way of promise, not a closed door for any people.

study.originalLanguages:
The word nasi in verse 16, translated 'princes,' comes from the verb nasa, to lift up, and describes someone raised to leadership. In Genesis 17:20 God used the same word when He promised that Ishmael would become 'the father of twelve rulers,' so verse 16 fulfils that promise in the same vocabulary. In Genesis 23:6 the Hittites called Abraham a nasi. In Numbers the word describes the leaders of each of Israel's twelve tribes, Numbers 1:16 and 7:2, and Ezekiel speaks of 'the princes of Kedar,' Ezekiel 27:21, using the same term for the leaders of Ishmael's firstborn line.

The twelve princes are listed 'by their tribes,' verse 16, using the word leom, a people or nation. The same word appears a few verses later when God tells Rebekah, 'two peoples from within you will be separated,' Genesis 25:23. Genesis uses the language of peoples and nations for both of Abraham's grandsons and for Ishmael's sons. The promise that Abraham would become 'a father of many nations,' Genesis 17:5, is visible in these lists.

Two words describe how the Ishmaelites lived. Chatserim, 'villages,' are unwalled settlements, and the word is used of the open villages of Kedar in Isaiah 42:11. Tirot, 'encampments,' are enclosed camps, and the same word describes the encampments of the Midianites that Israel burned in Numbers 31:10. The pair captures a people living between the desert and the settled lands.

The names themselves carry echoes. Ishmael means 'God hears,' as the BSB footnote on Genesis 16:11 explains, and one of his sons is Mishma, a name from the same root, shama, to hear. The last son, Kedemah, bears a name built on qedem, east, the direction of the desert peoples of 'the land of the east,' Genesis 25:6.

Verse 18 contains a difficult phrase. The verb 'settled' is shakan, to dwell, the same verb used in the angel's prophecy, 'he will live in hostility toward all his brothers,' Genesis 16:12. Then comes the phrase al penei kol echav, literally 'upon the face of all his brothers,' with the verb naphal, to fall. The expression al penei can mean 'in front of,' 'east of' or 'in defiance of,' and naphal can mean to fall upon, to settle, or even to die. The BSB takes it as hostility, echoing Genesis 16:12. Others read it as 'he settled alongside all his brothers.'

Finally, the word toledot in verse 12, 'account,' is related to the verb yalad, to bear or beget. It introduces a record of what came from a person. Ishmael's toledot is the seventh such heading in Genesis, and it is followed immediately by the eighth, Isaac's, verse 19.

typology.type: Ishmael and Isaac, the son of the flesh and the son of promise
typology.fulfillment: Paul sets the two sons side by side: 'His son by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, but his son by the free woman was born through the promise,' Galatians 4:23. Ishmael came by human planning, Isaac by God's power, Galatians 4:28-29. Paul uses them to illustrate two covenants, Sinai and the Jerusalem above. The escalation is that believers of every nation, 'like Isaac, are children of promise,' Galatians 4:28. The type falls short at one point: in Genesis the line of the flesh is an actual people whom God blesses, while in Paul it stands for a way of seeking God by human effort, which anyone of any nation may abandon for promise.

typology.type: The twelve princes of a line outside the covenant
typology.fulfillment: Ishmael's twelve princes stand beside the twelve sons of Jacob, Genesis 35:22-26, as a mirror image: a great people descended from Abraham but not the covenant people. Psalm 47:9 imagines a different outcome, 'The nobles of the nations have assembled as the people of the God of Abraham.' The escalation is that in Christ the princes of the nations join the people of Abraham's God rather than standing beside them. The correspondence is loose, and the New Testament does not draw it, so it is best seen as a hope that the prophets and psalms hold out and the gospel fulfils.

typology.type: The flocks of Kedar and the rams of Nebaioth on God's altar
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 60:7 pictures Ishmael's firstborn line, Nebaioth and Kedar, bringing their flocks to God's house: 'the rams of Nebaioth will serve you and go up on My altar with acceptance.' Paul speaks of his mission to the Gentiles as 'the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the Gentiles might become an offering acceptable to God,' Romans 15:16. The escalation is that the offering is no longer sheep and rams but the nations themselves, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. The type falls short because animal sacrifices could only picture acceptance, while Christ's sacrifice secures it.

typology.type: The son of the outsider, heard and blessed by God
typology.fulfillment: Ishmael was born to an Egyptian slave, named 'God hears,' Genesis 16:11, and blessed though not chosen. God heard the boy's voice in the wilderness, Genesis 21:17. In Christ those who were 'strangers to the covenants of the promise' are 'brought near through the blood of Christ,' Ephesians 2:12-13. Jesus speaks of 'other sheep that are not of this fold,' John 10:16. The escalation is from temporal blessing to adoption as children. The type falls short because Ishmael was blessed alongside the covenant, while those in Christ are brought into it.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first by showing that God's promises are reliable. Paul's great argument in Romans 9 begins, 'It is not as though God's word has failed,' Romans 9:6, and immediately cites the distinction between Ishmael and Isaac, 'Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned,' Romans 9:7. If God kept every detail of His word to Ishmael, the twelve princes, the great nation, even the hostility, then His word to Isaac, which leads to Christ, is certain. The promises to Abraham 'were spoken to Abraham and to his seed,' 'meaning One, who is Christ,' Galatians 3:16.

It leads to Christ by contrast between the two sons. Paul reads Ishmael and Isaac as a picture of two ways of relating to God: by the flesh, or by promise, Galatians 4:22-31. Ishmael was the son of human effort, Isaac the son of God's miraculous power. Christ is the ultimate son of promise, born not of human planning but by the power of the Spirit, Luke 1:35. And those who belong to Christ are also children of promise, Galatians 4:28.

It leads to Christ through the wideness of God's mercy. The prophets looked for a day when Ishmael's descendants would worship the LORD. Isaiah 42 is a striking example. It opens with the Servant of the LORD, 'My Chosen One,' who will 'bring justice to the nations,' Isaiah 42:1, and a few verses later it calls on 'the villages of Kedar' to sing a new song, Isaiah 42:11. Matthew applies that Servant passage directly to Jesus, 'In His name the nations will put their hope,' Matthew 12:18-21. The Servant who brings justice to the nations is the one who brings Kedar to praise.

Isaiah 60:7 goes further, picturing the flocks of Kedar and rams of Nebaioth accepted on God's altar. In Christ that picture becomes real. At Pentecost, 'Arabs' are among those who hear 'the wonders of God' in their own tongues, Acts 2:11. Paul himself went 'into Arabia' after his conversion, Galatians 1:17. Jesus said, 'I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them in as well,' John 10:16.

A caution is needed. The twelve princes of Ishmael are not a type of the twelve apostles, and the names in the list do not hide messages about Christ. The number twelve in the Gospels points back to Israel's twelve tribes, not to Ishmael. What the passage gives is the faithfulness of God's word and a glimpse of the peoples whom God's mercy in Christ would one day reach.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who keeps every word He speaks. He had made promises about Ishmael before his birth, Genesis 16:10-12, at the covenant of circumcision, Genesis 17:20, and in the wilderness, Genesis 21:13 and 21:18. Each is fulfilled here: the numberless offspring, the twelve princes, the great nation, even the hostility. God's faithfulness is not selective. He keeps His lesser promises as carefully as His great ones.

He is the God who hears. Ishmael's name means 'God hears,' Genesis 16:11, given because 'the LORD has heard your cry of affliction.' When the boy was dying of thirst, 'God heard the voice of the boy where he lies,' Genesis 21:17. And when Abraham prayed, 'O that Ishmael might live under Your blessing,' God answered, 'As for Ishmael, I have heard you,' Genesis 17:18 and 17:20. The list of twelve princes is the long answer to a father's prayer and a slave woman's cry.

He is sovereign in election. God chose Isaac, not Ishmael, to carry the covenant, Genesis 17:21, and Paul later explains that this choice rests on God's call, not on birth or merit, Romans 9:7-13. The passage shows that election is real and that it runs through one line.

Yet He is also generous beyond election. The same God who chose Isaac blessed Ishmael, made him fruitful and gave his descendants a territory. Paul says God 'determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands,' Acts 17:26, and the 'from Havilah to Shur' of verse 18 is part of that divine ordering. Deuteronomy 32:8 says the Most High 'set the boundaries of the peoples.' God rules the nations who are not His covenant people as surely as He rules Israel.

He is also truthful about hard things. The prophecy that Ishmael would 'live in hostility toward all his brothers,' Genesis 16:12, was not a pleasant word, and God kept it too. God's faithfulness includes His honesty about the brokenness that sin brings into families and nations.

For worship, the passage invites trust and breadth. If God kept every promise to Ishmael, His people can trust every promise to them in Christ, 2 Corinthians 1:20. And if God's care reached the tents of Kedar, His people should share His heart for the nations, praying for the day when 'a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue,' will stand before the Lamb, Revelation 7:9.

crossReferences.note: Before Ishmael was born, the angel promised Hagar numberless offspring and foretold that her son 'will live in hostility toward all his brothers.' Genesis 25:16-18 fulfils both halves of the prophecy, the fruitfulness and the hostility, closing Ishmael's story as it began.

God answered Abraham's prayer for Ishmael: 'I will surely bless him... He will become the father of twelve rulers, and I will make him into a great nation.' The twelve princes of Genesis 25:16 are the exact fulfilment, using the same Hebrew word nasi.

In the wilderness God 'heard the voice of the boy' and promised, 'I will make him into a great nation.' The list of twelve tribes shows the dying boy of Genesis 21 becoming the father of peoples, a monument to the God who hears.

Esau marries 'Mahalath, the sister of Nebaioth and daughter of Abraham's son Ishmael.' The firstborn of Ishmael's twelve sons is named, and the two lines outside the covenant, Esau's and Ishmael's, are joined by marriage.

A caravan of Ishmaelites carrying spices, balm and myrrh buys Joseph and takes him to Egypt. The trading life of Ishmael's descendants, described in Genesis 25:16-18, becomes the means by which God sends Joseph ahead to save his family.

The prophet calls on 'the villages of Kedar' to raise their voices and sing a new song to the LORD. This comes in the chapter that opens with the Servant who brings justice to the nations, Isaiah 42:1, whom Matthew identifies as Jesus, Matthew 12:18-21.

'All the flocks of Kedar will be gathered to you; the rams of Nebaioth will serve you and go up on My altar with acceptance.' Ishmael's first two sons, named in Genesis 25:13, are pictured in the age to come as worshippers at God's house.

'The nobles of the nations have assembled as the people of the God of Abraham.' The psalm pictures the leaders of other nations, like Ishmael's twelve princes, gathered not beside God's people but as part of them, worshipping the God of their common ancestor.

Paul contrasts the son 'born according to the flesh' with the son 'born through the promise,' using Ishmael and Isaac to illustrate two covenants. Believers are children of promise, like Isaac, Galatians 4:28, and the way of the flesh cannot inherit.

Paul insists that God's word has not failed, because 'not all who are descended from Israel are Israel.' He cites 'Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned,' Genesis 21:12. The separation of Ishmael's toledot from Isaac's illustrates God's electing purpose.

At Pentecost 'Cretans and Arabs' hear the apostles declaring the wonders of God in their own tongues. The peoples of the Arabian desert, among whom Ishmael's descendants settled, are present when the gospel first goes out to the nations.

God 'determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands.' The territory 'from Havilah to Shur' in Genesis 25:18 is part of that ordering. God sets the bounds of peoples outside the covenant as surely as He gives Canaan to Israel.

study.oneStory:
At creation God blessed humanity and told them to be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth, Genesis 1:28. After the flood the nations spread out according to their families, Genesis 10:32, and then at Babel humanity was scattered, Genesis 11:9. God's answer to the scattering was to call Abraham, promising that 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you,' Genesis 12:3. The line of Ishmael is one of those families, and its twelve princes are a living proof that God keeps His word.

The passage answers promises made earlier in the story, to Hagar in Genesis 16, to Abraham in Genesis 17 and in the wilderness in Genesis 21. It also shows that God's blessing is not limited to the covenant line. Ishmael is fruitful, becomes a great nation and is buried with the same honour as his father. God's kindness reaches beyond the chosen family.

The passage also sets up what follows. The story now narrows to Isaac, then to Jacob, then to Judah and David, and finally to one descendant, Christ. Ishmael's descendants remain on the edge of the story, sometimes as traders, sometimes as enemies, and sometimes in the prophets' visions as worshippers. The hostility of verse 18 is a reminder that the fracture of Genesis 3 runs through Abraham's own family.

In Christ the story turns. He is the promised seed, and through Him the blessing of Abraham reaches the nations, Galatians 3:14. The line of the flesh and the line of promise are no longer marked by ancestry, since all who believe, of any people, are children of promise, Galatians 3:7 and 4:28. At Pentecost Arabs hear the gospel, Acts 2:11, and the mission to the nations begins.

The new creation fulfils the prophets' hope. Isaiah saw the flocks of Kedar and the rams of Nebaioth on God's altar, Isaiah 60:7, and John sees the nations walking by the light of the Lamb and bringing their glory into the city, Revelation 21:24-26. The descendants of Ishmael who lived in hostility toward their brothers will be among the multitude from every nation and tribe who stand before the throne as one people, Revelation 7:9.

quiz.q: What is significant about Ishmael having twelve sons who became princes?

options.text: It fulfils God's specific promise to make Ishmael a great nation with twelve princes.
options.note: The twelve princes match the promises of Genesis 17:20 and 21:18.

options.text: It shows Ishmael was wealthier than Isaac.
options.note: The point is the fulfilled promise, not a comparison of wealth.

options.text: It proves Ishmael was the true covenant heir.
options.note: The covenant runs through Isaac; Ishmael is blessed but not the heir.

options.text: It is simply a list with no particular meaning.
options.note: The twelve princes deliberately fulfil God's earlier word.

quiz.q: Why does Scripture pause to record Ishmael's line here?

options.text: To show God faithfully kept His promise to Ishmael before the story narrows to Isaac.
options.note: The record honours God's word to Ishmael and clears the way for the covenant line.

options.text: To argue that Ishmael's descendants should rule over Isaac's.
options.note: It notes their settlement and tension, but the aim is to show God's faithfulness, not a claim to rule.

options.text: To replace Isaac with Ishmael in the covenant.
options.note: The covenant remains with Isaac; Ishmael is honoured but not chosen as heir.

options.text: To condemn Ishmael and his descendants.
options.note: The passage honours God's blessing on Ishmael rather than condemning him.

quiz.q: What does the fulfilment of God's promise to Ishmael reveal about God?

options.text: That God is faithful to every word He speaks, even outside the chosen line.
options.note: God keeps His promises to Ishmael as surely as to Isaac.

options.text: That God's promises apply only to the covenant family.
options.note: The opposite; the passage shows God keeping a promise to one outside the covenant line.

options.text: That God changes His mind depending on circumstances.
options.note: God's constancy is on display; He does exactly what He said.

options.text: That God had forgotten Ishmael after Isaac was born.
options.note: God remembers Ishmael and fulfils His word to him.

quiz.q: How does honouring Ishmael fit the larger story leading to Christ?

options.text: The line narrows through Isaac toward Christ, while God's mercy to Ishmael hints at grace reaching the outsider.
options.note: The chosen line and the wideness of mercy stand together, both fulfilled in Christ.

options.text: It shows the promise to bless the nations was abandoned.
options.note: The promise continues through Isaac; God's mercy to Ishmael actually foreshadows its breadth.

options.text: It means there is no chosen line at all.
options.note: There is a clear chosen line through Isaac; Ishmael is blessed alongside it.

options.text: It proves God's mercy is limited to one family forever.
options.note: The care shown to Ishmael points to a mercy that in Christ reaches the far off.

questions: God kept His promise to Ishmael, a son outside the covenant line. How does it comfort you to know that God does not forget anyone He has made a promise to?
The story honours Ishmael even as it moves on through Isaac. Where do you need to trust God's larger plan even when you are not at the centre of it?
God's mercy reached a son of the outsider. Who in your life feels far off from God, and how might His wide mercy be at work in them?
Ishmael's descendants lived in tension with their kin. Is there family tension in your own story that you long to bring before the God who cares for all sides?
God's promises never fall to the ground. Which promise of God do you most need to lean on this week, trusting that He keeps His word?

translationNotes.note: The closing clause renders a Hebrew idiom, literally he fell or settled over against all his brothers, describing Ishmael's descendants dwelling apart and in tension with their kin.
